KEY POINTS

Living things have been divided into two main groups; the plants and animals. • Plants make their own food whereas, animals depend on plants or other animals for food. • Both plants and animals need food, sunlight, water and air. • The animals have been divided into two groups; the vertebrates and invertebrates. • The plants have been divided into two major groups; the flowering and non-flowering plants.
KEY POINTS
• The number of various types of living things found at a particular place is called biodiversity. • Teeth, bones, lungs, heart, stomach, muscles and brain are the major parts of the human body.
KEY POINTS

• Different parts of animal body have specific functions for example, teeth to chew food, bones to protect and support body parts, lungs to bring air into the body, heart to circulate blood in the body, stomach to digest food, muscles to move body and brain controls the functions of other body parts. • Root, stem, leaf, flower and seed are the major parts of plant.
KEY POINTS

• The function of roots is to anchor the plant into the ground and absorb water and minerals from the soil. • The function of stem is to transport water and food. • The function of leaves is to make food and produce oxygen. • The function of flowers is to produce seed and the function of seeds is to produce new plants.

Chapter 2: Ecosystem
Are the living organisms affected by non-living things? • Are the seeds living things? • Why are the habitats of living organisms different from one another
Students' Learning Outcomes
After studying this chapter, the students will be able to:
Students' Learning Outcomes

Recognize what is an ecosystem (e.g., forests, ponds, rivers, grasslands and deserts). • Explain biotic (plants, animals and humans) and abiotic factor (light, temperature, soil and water) and their linkages. • Analyse the way these biotic and abiotic constituents create a balance to sustain any ecosystem.
Students' Learning Outcomes

• Recognize the interactions between animals and plants and the importance of maintaining balance within an ecosystem. • Describe a few food chains and analyse their structure to understand their function. • Describe the role of living things at each link in a simple food chain (e.g., plants produce their own food; some animals eat plants, while other animals eat the animals that eat plants).
Students' Learning Outcomes

• Identify and describe common predators and their prey. • Recognize and explain that some living things in an ecosystem compete with each other for food and space. • Recognize the value of a balanced ecosystem. • Interpret that human actions such as urbanization, pollution and deforestation affect food chains in an ecosystem. • Identify various actions and roles that humans can play in preserving various ecosystems.
Environment and Ecosystem

If we look around, we see variety of living and non-living things. The environment can be defined as a sum of all living and non-living things around an organism. The living and non-living components of an environment interact with each other.
Environment and Ecosystem

Every living things lives in a particular environment. Fish lives in water, tiger lives in forest whereas human beings live in villages and cities. The birds make nests on the trees and the ants live underground in nests. Do you know other animals that live in particular environments?

Fish | Ant | Parrot; Bird's nest | Pond | Anthill
Ecosystem

The living and non-living components of any environment make the ecosystem. Various types of ecosystems are found on our earth for example, forest, grassland, ocean, river, pond, snowy areas and desert.

Components of Ecosystem
There are two components of an ecosystem. 1. Abiotic 2. Biotic
Abiotic Components
The non-living components of an ecosystem are called abiotic components. These include temperature, air, water, light and soil.
Biotic Components
The living components of an ecosystem are called biotic components. The biotic components are divided into three groups, which are given below:
1. Producer

The plants produce food for themselves and for animals with the help of absorbed water and sunlight. That is why, they are called producers. All the plants e.g., herbs, climbers, shrubs and trees are producers. Aquatic plants (for example lotus), algae are also producers. These are a major source of food for the aquatic animals.
2. Consumer

The living things which obtain their food from other living things are called consumers. They cannot make their own food. They depend on plants and other animals for their food. All the animals are consumers.
3. Decomposer
The living things which breakdown the dead bodies of plants and animals into simple components for their food from these, are called decomposers. Bacteria and fungi are main decomposers.
3. Decomposer
Producer | Consumer | Decomposers; lotus plants; garden plants | a heron catching a fish; a panda eating bamboo | bacteria; a mushroom

Balanced Ecosystem

The Sun is the main source of energy in an ecosystem. The plants make food with the help of sunlight, carbon dioxide and water. They also produce oxygen in this process. This oxygen is used by animals for respiration. During respiration, animals produce carbon dioxide which is used by plants to make food. Such self-sustaining and durable ecosystem is called balanced ecosystem.
Balanced Ecosystem
All the living things are essential for one another. They affect the lives of one another. Some animals benefit or harm one another.
Food Chain
To obtain food living things depend on one another. Plants make food with the help of sunlight and water. The animals which eat plants are called herbivores, for example rabbit, goat, deer and cow.
Food Chain
The animals which eat other animals are called carnivores, for example lion, tiger, crocodile and shark.
Food Chain
The animals which eat both plants and animals are called omnivores for example man, bear, birds and crow, etc.
Food Chain

Producers make food, which is used by herbivores. The herbivores are eaten by carnivores. These carnivores may be eaten by other carnivores. The series of eating and being eaten in an ecosystem is called food chain. Grasshopper eats a plant and is eaten by rat. The rat becomes a prey of owl. This is an example of food chain.
Links of Food Chain
A food chain consists of three links.
Links of Food Chain

1. In any food chain the first living thing is a producer (for example plant and algae). • 2. The second main link is the herbivores animal for example rat, zebra and goat. • 3. The third main link is a carnivores for example lion, fox and snake.
Predator- Prey Relationship

The animal which eats by killing another living things is called a predator for example lion, tiger, shark and lizard. The living thing which is killed and eaten by the predator is called a prey, for example zebra, deer, rat and fish. The interaction between predator and prey is called predation. For example, deer is killed and eaten by lion. Here, lion is the predator and deer is its prey.
Predator- Prey Relationship
Similarly, goat is predator and grass is its prey.
Competition among Organisms

All the organisms living in an ecosystem depend on the resources which are available in that area. Every area can provide food and place to a limited number of living things. The limited resources in an ecosystem compel the living things to compete for food and place. For example, in the grassland all the herbivores compete for grass.
Impacts of Human Actions on Food Chain in an Ecosystem

In the ancient times, human actions had little impact on their environment. Now a days, there are very visible impacts of human beings on environment. After the increase in the population, humans established cities. For this purpose, they cut forests, built roads and factories. These actions polluted the environment and water resources.
Impacts of Human Actions on Food Chain in an Ecosystem

Human beings did irreversible damage to the ecosystem of the land and ocean. The cutting of forests destroyed the habitats of wildlife. Human beings also started unnecessary hunting of animals. Because of all such activities of human beings many wild organisms have become extinct and many others have become endangered.
Role of Human to Save the Ecosystem
Humans have done irreversible damage to the environment, but they are trying to save the ecosystem as well. Do you know what they are doing?
Role of Human to Save the Ecosystem

1. Wildlife parks have been made to save the habitats of living things, e.g. Margalla National Park. • 2. Tree plantation is being done and artificial forests are being created to provide the natural habitat to living things. • 3. Awareness is being created to save the environment and habitats of living things.

Do you know?
Plantation Day: Plantation day can be observed everyday but in the schools of Pakistan it is celebrated in August as 'week of tree plantation'.

States of Matter and Arrangement of Particles
Matter consists of very tiny particles. The arrangement of particles in solid, liquid and gas is different.
Arrangement of Particles in Solids

In solid, the particles are strongly attached with each other. These particles have strong forces of attraction. The particles vibrate to and fro about their mean position. Solids cannot be easily pressed. Solids maintain their definite shape and volume.
Arrangement of Particles in Solids
The shape of the solid will remain same and wooden piece would not come out of the hole due to its fixed shape.
Arrangement of Particles in Liquid

The particles of liquid are near each other. The forces of attraction among them are weaker than in solids. The particles keep on colliding with one another. Their particles can move near or far from one another and thus liquids can flow.
Arrangement of Particles in Liquid
The volume of liquids is definite, but their shape is not definite. The liquid takes the shape of the vessel in which it is poured. We have done this in activity 4.1.
Arrangement of Particles in Liquid
The water flows out of the hole due to weak forces of attraction among the particles of water, therefore, they can flow fast. That's why the shape of the liquid is not definite.
Arrangement of Particles in Gas

The particles in a gas are much farther apart from one another. They move fast because of weaker forces of attraction. The gas particles can move freely in all directions. They occupy all the available space. That is why they have no definite shape and volume.

Energy and its Sources

The ability to do work is called energy. Energy is used in the movements of humans and animals, light in the bulb, heat in the heater and sound of the school bell. From where do we get energy? The biggest source of energy is the Sun. On the Earth, we see the energy of the Sun as light and we feel it as heat. The flowing water, air, coal, oil, gas and wood are also the sources of energy.
Energy and its Sources
Coal | Wood | Fast Flowing Water | Oil | Natural Gas
Energy and its Sources
Let's look at different sources of energy.

Transformation of Energy

In our daily lives, we see that one form of energy can be transformed into another form. Electricity is produced from the fast-flowing water. It is called as hydroelectricity. For this purpose, a dam is built. The water of river is stored in a lake at a certain height. From there, the water flows very fast through a tunnel. The energy in the flowing water runs a turbine.
Transformation of Energy
The turbine runs a generator which produces electricity.
Transformation of Energy
In thermal power station, we burn coal, oil or gas to change water into steam. This steam is used to run a turbine. The turbine runs a generator to produce electricity.
Do you know?
In windmill, electricity is produced from the energy of fast wind.
Conservation of Energy

There are limited reserves of the sources of energy like coal, oil and gas. We cannot increase the amounts of such sources because these are made in millions of years. However, we can save these sources. For this, we have to use them carefully. The energy sources cannot support us for long time to fulfil the needs of energy for fast growing population.
Conservation of Energy

We need to make a balance between facilities needed for better life and the supply of energy. Therefore, we need to create awareness among people to use the present sources carefully. We should also try to explore new sources of energy so that we and next generations have not to face problems of energy shortage.
Light

Light is a form of energy that helps us to see things around us. The Sun, stars and lightning are the natural sources of light. Candle, oil lamp, torch, electric bulb etc. are the artificial sources of light. When light leaves its source, it travels in all directions in straight lines. Light can pass through some objects. When light cannot pass through an object, a shadow of that object is formed behind it.

Rainbow

There are seven colours in sunlight (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). After rain, some drops of water are suspended in the air. When sunlight passes through water droplets, they divide it into seven colours like a prism. This is called rainbow.
Sound Energy
Sound is the form of energy that is produced by vibrations in an object. These vibrations reach our ears through the particles of the air. In this way, we hear sound.

Sound Energy
The vibrating object produces sound. Sound needs some medium to travel. Most of the sounds reach us by travelling through air.
Do you know?
When we speak, the vocal cords present in our throat vibrate and produce sound.
Interesting Information
Sound cannot travel in space. This is the reason that we cannot hear the sound of explosions in the Sun.
Sound Energy
Like light, sound also reflects. When sound bounces back from an object at a certain distance and we hear it again, it is called echo.
Interesting Information
Bat uses echo to catch its prey in darkness. It emits sound from its mouth. By using echo of its sound, it find the way in darkness to reach the prey.
Do you know?
A hard and smooth object reflects sound better.
Do you know?
To hear a clear echo, the reflecting surface should be at least 17 metres away from the source of sound.
Heat

Heat is a form of energy that always travels from a hot object to the cold object. We use the term "temperature" to measure the hotness or coldness of an object. The temperature of an object shows how much hot or cold that object is. The instrument used to measure temperature is called thermometer.
Thermometer and Different Units of Temperature

When the bulb of a thermometer touches a hot object, the mercury or alcohol present in its bulb expands. So, it rises in the glass tube of thermometer. Similarly, when the bulb touches a cold object, the mercury or alcohol contracts. So, it falls down in the glass tube of thermometer.
Thermometer and Different Units of Temperature

Doctors usually measure temperature in Fahrenheit scale. It is represented as °F. Degree centigrade is also a unit of temperature. It is written as °C. We usually use degree centigrade unit to describe the condition of weather.
Electrical Energy

Electricity or electrical energy is produced by generators. This electricity is supplied to our homes through wires. Cells and batteries are also the sources of electrical energy. These are used in toys, torch, clock and remote control etc. We use electrical energy for running many devices in our homes. Electrical energy can be transformed into other forms of energy like heat, light and sound.
Electrical Energy
In heater, the electrical energy changes into heat. | In electric bulb, the electrical energy changes into light. | In loud speaker, the electrical energy changes into sound.

Sources of energy are sun, flowing water, wind, coal, oil, gas etc. • The system of life is working due to transformations of one form of energy into another. • The natural sources of energy are limited. Therefore, we should use the energy wisely. • The Sun is the biggest source of energy on Earth. • Light helps us to see things. We see shadows, images and rainbow due to light.

• Sound is produced by vibrating objects. • Echo is the sound that is heard after the sound bounces back from an object.

Chapter 6: Force and Motion
Why are different bodies sometime found in a state of rest and motion? • If an object is thrown upwards, why does it always return to the Earth? • What is the importance of gear in a bicycle?
Students' Learning Outcomes
After studying this chapter, the students will be able to:
Students' Learning Outcomes

Describe force and motion with examples from daily life. • Identify gravity as a force that draws objects to Earth. • Investigate that friction works against the direction of motion. • Provide reasoning with evidence that friction can be either detrimental or useful under different circumstances.
Students' Learning Outcomes

• Recognize that simple machines, (e.g., levers, pulleys, gears, ramps) help make motion easier (e.g., make lifting things easier, reduce the amount of force required, change the distance or change the direction of the force).
Force

Have a look at your surroundings. You will notice that some objects are stationary and some are moving. Can you tell how to produce motion in the bodies at rest? For example, how can a toy car be moved? When you push or pull the toy car with your hand, it causes the toy car to move.
Force
The act of pushing or pulling a body is called force. Force is used to move or stop the body. For example, to open a door, we either pull it towards us or push it away.
Force

In fact push or pull are forces. Force increases or decreases the speed of a body. Force can also change the direction of motion. For example, applying force to a ball with a bat changes its direction of motion.
Force
a man pulling a door open | a batsman hitting the ball with a bat
Do you know?
When you pick up an object, you are pulling it. When you throw an object, you are pushing it.
Force
A force acting on a body can change its shape. For example, if we press an empty can, it will be compressed.
Force
an empty can | the can crushed in a hand

Motion
You may have seen different types of swings in a park or playground. How do they move?
Motion
The see-saw moves up and down. The merry-go-round moves in a circle while the swing moves back and forth. What do you observe from it?
Motion

The body changes its position during movement. For example, a see-saw is in a state of rest in the park. Children sitting on see-saw apply force on it and see-saw starts moving up and down. The process in which a body changes its position is called motion.

Gravity
Look at the following pictures and tell:
Gravity
a fountain in a pond | a tree dropping its leaves | a footballer kicking a ball upward; the ball rises and falls back
Gravity
You may have noticed that whatever is thrown upward, it returns to the ground. The Earth actually pulls bodies towards itself with a specific force. This force is called gravity of the Earth.
Friction
You have often observed that when you kick a football, it stops after covering a certain distance. Why does it stop? Certainly, there is a force acting on football that stops it. What force is this?
Friction
Friction is the force that stops or tends to stop moving objects. Friction occurs when a body moves in contact with another body. Friction always acts against the direction of movement.
Advantages of Friction

Friction plays very important role in our daily life. Igniting of the match stick, penetration of the nail into the wood or wall, slowing down of the vehicles and eventually stopping are all possible due to friction.
Advantages of Friction
striking a match stick | cars slowing down and stopping on a road | a nail driven into a block of wood
Do you know?
We cannot walk on Earth without friction. If there is less friction, it becomes difficult to walk.

Disadvantages of Friction

Friction is very useful in our daily life but sometimes it can be harmful. For example, friction causes our shoes to wear out. Due to friction, the tyres of the car not only get worn over time but sometimes they can even burst.
Disadvantages of Friction
worn-out shoe soles | worn car tyres
Disadvantages of Friction
Similarly, friction causes wear and tear of moving parts of machines over time and the machines become unusable.
Do you know?
The worn tyre of the vehicle must be replaced otherwise the risk of accidents increases.
Simple Machines

The use of machines in our lives is increasing day by day. What is the reason for this? Everything that makes our work easier is called a machine. Machines make our work easier by changing the amount and direction of force. Lever, pulley, gear and ramp (inclined plane) are simple machines.
Do you know?
Modern machines, such as cars or watches, are made up of simple machines. Each machine has to be provided energy constantly to keep it working.
Lever
A lever is a simple machine that can be used to push or lift heavy objects. The lever is like a simple rod that turns around a certain point called fulcrum.
Lever
By applying force (effort) to one end of the lever, the weight (load) at the other end is lifted.

In this activity, pencil will act as fulcrum while the book will be a weight (load) which can be easily lifted with the help of force (effort).
Pulley
A pulley is a simple machine, consists of a grooved wheel and a rope. The load is lifted up by applying force (effort) on one end of the rope passing over the pulley.
Pulley

As pulling a weight is easier than lifting it so the machine can easily lift heavy objects. For example, water can be easily drawn from a well by using pulley. The flag is raised up with the help of pulley. For this, when you pull the rope down, it lifts the flag upwards.
Pulley
a girl raising the Pakistan flag on a flagpole | a boy drawing a bucket of water from a well
Pulley
Changing the direction of force makes it easier to work with the pulley. For example, if we want to lift heavy objects with the help of pulley, we have to put the effort downwards.
Gear

Gear is a simple machine which consists of toothed wheels of different sizes. The teeth of these wheels fit in with each other and move together. With the help of gears, we can increase or decrease the speed.
Gear
In everyday life, gears of various sizes are used in bicycles, grinders and sugarcane juice machines.
Ramp (Inclined Plane)

Inclined plane is a simple machine with one end relatively higher than the other. It requires less force and energy to move objects from one place to another. It allows us to move objects easily from bottom to top and top to bottom. The pictures show different types of inclined planes.

The process of pushing or pulling of a body is called force. • The process in which a body changes its position is called motion. • The Earth pulls bodies towards itself with a specific force. This force is called gravity. • Friction is the force that stops or tends to stop moving objects.
Key Points

• Igniting of a match stick and walking on ground are the advantages of friction while wear out of tyres and parts of machines are the disadvantages of friction. • Lever, pulley, gear and inclined plane are simple machines that make our work easier.

Chapter 7: Earth and it's Resources
From where do oceans get water? • Dead animals are decomposed, then where do their skeletons kept in the museum come from? • Do living organisms in the soil breathe?
Students' Learning Outcomes

Students' Learning Outcomes

Recognize that Earth's surface is made up of land and water and is surrounded by air. • Recognize that water in rivers and streams flows from mountains to oceans or lakes. • Identify some of Earth's natural resources (e.g., water, wind, soil, forests, oil, natural gas, minerals) that are used in everyday life.
Students' Learning Outcomes

• Recognize that some remains (fossils) of animals and plants that lived on the Earth, a long time ago, are found in rocks, soil and under the sea. • Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable resources. • Investigate the impact of human activities on the Earth's natural resources. • Suggest the ways to conserve the natural resources.
Natural Resources

Many of us do not know the importance of natural resources. We hardly ever thought about the basic sources of our daily used required items. We obtain the basic material for making necessary items of life from land, sea or air.
Natural Resources
"The basic material that humans get from land, sea or air are called natural resources."
Natural Resources
There is no substitute for natural resources. If humans do not use these resources properly, there is a danger that these will be unavailable soon.
For Your Information
About 11% of the land is cultivated in the world.
Earth and its Physical Characteristics

If you look at the globe of the Earth, you will see that most of the area is blue which represents water. You will see a small as green or light brown (Khaki) which indicates land. The Earth's surface consists of land and water. The Earth is surrounded by air. About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water and the remaining 29% is land. Although we do not see air but it is present everywhere on the Earth.
Earth and its Physical Characteristics
Air is present even in soil and water.

Earth and its Physical Characteristics
Air entered the bottle, through the hole in the bottle and inflated the balloon. It means that air is present everywhere around us.
Distribution of Water on Earth's Surface

About 97% of the water present on Earth is in the oceans. The remaining 3% is present in glaciers, rivers, streams and lakes. Rainwater is added in rivers and streams. From here, the water flows to lakes and oceans. The snow falling on mountains also melts and becomes water. This water also flows to rivers and streams and finally falls into the lakes and oceans.
Earth's Resources

The Earth is rich in many resources including water, air, soil, forests, coal, oil, natural gas and minerals, etc. We use natural resources to make different things in our daily life. The properties of natural resources make them useful for a variety of purposes. For example, clay is used to make bricks and pottery while sand is commonly used to make buildings and glass.
Do you know?
The pencil in your geometry box is made from the wood of a tree while the rubber is obtained from the secretion of a rubber tree.
Earth's Resources
Let us understand some important natural resources and their importance in daily life:
Water

All living things need water to survive. We use water for drinking, cooking and washing clothes and dishes. Water is also very important for plants and crops. Running water is also used to generate electricity.
Water
water poured into a glass for drinking | watering plants with a hose pipe

Air bubbles start coming out of the soil. This proves that there is air in the soil.
Air

Air is very important for the survival of life on Earth. Air is present all around the Earth's surface. It is also present in soil and water due to which living beings can breathe inside soil and water. Fast blowing air is also used to generate electricity.
Air
a wind turbine generating electricity | a fish breathing in water
Soil

Soil is the outer layer of the Earth which contains water, air, fertile matter and gravel. Soil provides essential nutrients to plants for growth. It also provides shelter to many organisms. It is also used to make bricks, glass and utensils.
Interesting Information
World Soil Day is celebrated on 5th December every year.
Soil
crops (sugarcane) growing in soil | hands shaping a clay pot
Forests

The part of the Earth that is completely covered with trees is called a forest. Forests not only provide us timber but are also natural habitats for animals. They also provide us fresh and oxygenated air.
Do you know?
Forests cover 5.2% of the total area of Pakistan. Pakistan's largest natural forest is located in the city of Ziarat in Balochistan province.
Natural Oil
Crude oil found underground, is a major source of energy for humans. We use this oil as fuel in vehicles and other means of transport. We also generate electricity by burning this oil.
Interesting Information
We produce kerosene, petrol, diesel, engine oil, grease, petroleum jelly and coaltar from the crude oil which we get from the Earth.
Natural Gas

Natural gas is obtained from the Earth and is used for heating and to generate electricity. Natural gas is used as a fuel for cooking in homes. It is also used to make fertilizers. Coal is also an important natural resource that is used as a fuel.

Minerals

Minerals are simple solid chemical substances which are present in the Earth. They are obtained by digging the Earth. Gold, silver, copper, iron and salt, etc. are all minerals. They are used to make many items such as wires, coins, jewellery and utensils.

Non-Renewable Resources

Some natural resources such as coal, petrol, diesel and natural gas take millions of years to form. Such limited resources are called non-renewable resources. Once they are used, they can not be replaced by new ones easily.
Non-Renewable Resources
Natural gas | Coal | Petrol
Renewable Resources

Those unlimited resources which can be replaced after use are called renewable resources. Air, water, soil, forests and solar energy are renewable resources. Some of these resources are also used as fuel substitutes.
Renewable Resources
Solar energy | Wind energy | Water energy
Effect of Human Activities on Natural Resources

The lavish use of natural resources is causing irreparable damage to our environment. Growing population, excessive use of fossil fuels and deforestation, etc. are rapidly reducing land resources. Due to it, humans are facing problems such as climatic change, pollution and lack of clean drinking water.
Effect of Human Activities on Natural Resources

If we do not use natural resources carefully then a stage will come when renewable resources like trees, animals, soil, water and air will also run out or will become unusable. That is why the careful use of natural resources and their preservation is very essential.

Chapter 8: Earth's Weather and Climate
How do weathers change? • Why climate of the Earth is different at different locations? • Why do hilly areas become spots of recreation during summer?
Students' Learning Outcomes
After studying this chapter, the students will be able to:
Students' Learning Outcomes

Understand the difference between weather and climate. • Relate that weather changes (i.e. daily variation in temperature, humidity, precipitation in the form of rain or snow, clouds and wind) with changing geographical location. • Recognize that average temperature and precipitation can change with seasons and location.
Students' Learning Outcomes

In our daily life, we observe that sometime it rains, sometime it is sunny, sometime the weather becomes cold and pleasant and sometime it becomes hot. Occasionally, this weather change occurs suddenly and sometimes it takes many days. Sunlight, air pressure, rain and cloud etc. play important role in the change of weather.
Weather and Climate

The daily condition of the environment or atmosphere of a location is called its weather. The duration of weather may be one or many days. Weather is described in terms of temperature, humidity in air, precipitation (rain or snow), clouds and winds of that particular location.
Do you know?
Annual rotation of the Earth around the Sun and the tilt of the Earth on its axis are responsible for changes in the weather.
Weather and Climate
Rain | Intensive sun (summer) | Storm
Weather and Climate

Is your region hot or cold? The general conditions of an area are called climate. It is the average weather conditions of an area. In fact climate describes the general and long-lasting weather conditions of an area.
Do you know?
The study of weather conditions is called Meteorology. The people related to this study are known as Meteorologists.
Difference between Weather and Climate

Weather: Short duration conditions of an environment. For example; Yesterday, the weather was a little cold. | Climate: Average long duration conditions of weather. For example; This year, it is expected that Monsoon rains will begin early.
Do you know?

The climate of a region affects the living habits, diet, growth and colour of people. In the regions of cold climate, people wear warm dresses, sweaters and gloves while, people of the regions of hot climate wear thin and light dresses.
Interesting Information
Weather conditions are described by using the following instruments:
Interesting Information

Barometer | Anemometer | Rain Gauge | Thermometer; Instrument to measure the air pressure | Instrument to measure the speed and direction of wind | Instrument to measure the amount of rain | Instrument to measure the temperature of air
Difference between Weather and Climate

The movement of winds and clouds in the upper atmosphere of a region helps us to predict the change in weather conditions for the next few days. Meteorologists (weather experts) keep us informed about changes in the weather for the next few days. They provide us information about rain, wind or storm etc. in advance.

Interesting Information
The maximum day temperature of 58 degree Centigrade was recorded in 1922 in the desert of Libya (Africa).
Relationship between Geographical Location and Climate

Geographical location of a region is an important factor for determining its climate. Many other factors affect the climate of any geographical location. These include temperature, air pressure, speed and direction of wind, humidity, rain and snow. Have you ever thought why does the weather change with the arrival of spring, summer or winter?
Relationship between Geographical Location and Climate
The climate or weather changes of any region depend upon falling of Sun rays vertically or slanting.
Do you know?
The maximum temperature in Pakistan was 53.7°C in Turbat (Baluchistan) on 28th May, 2017 and was 53.5°C in Mohenjo Daro (Sindh) on 26th May, 2010.
Do you know?
The Equator is an imaginary line that divides the Earth into two equal parts.
Relationship between Geographical Location and Climate
On the basis of climate, we can divide the Earth into three zones: 1. Tropical Zone 2. Temperate Zone 3. Polar Zone
1. Tropical Zone
Tropical Zone consists of the regions located around the equator. Here, the Sun rays fall vertically. That is why, the climate of this zone is hot.
2. Temperate Zone
Temperate Zone is located between Tropical and Polar Zones. Here, the Sun rays fall slant. The climate of this zone is mild due to weak Sun rays.
3. Polar Zone
It consists of the areas around the north and south poles of the Earth. Here, the Sun rays are more slanted and weak. Therefore, the climate of this Zone is the coldest.
3. Polar Zone
As we move away from the equator, the climate becomes less hot. Eventually, the temperature is minimum at the poles, hence these are the coldest regions of the Earth.
Interesting Information
Waterbodies make the climate of the adjacent land areas mild. • With the rise of height from the sea level, the climate becomes cooler and the duration of winter season increases.
Do you know?
The minimum temperature in Pakistan was –18 degree Centigrade in Quetta on 8th January 1970 whereas it was -51 degree Centigrade at K-2 peak.
Global Change in Climate

The heat, smoke and gases released from factories, vehicles and other human activities not only pollute our environment but also cause an increase in the average temperature of the Earth. It is called global warming. Global warming is very harmful for climate and life on land and in water.

Moon

The brightest objects appearing in the sky after the Sun is the Moon. It is a natural satellite of the Earth. Moon completes one revolution around the Earth in about 29.5 days. We see the Moon almost in a new shape everyday. Sometime, we see a very thin Moon which is called crescent. Sometime, we see a complete Moon which is called Full Moon (badar).
Moon

Among all celestial bodies, Moon is the closest to the Earth. It is at a distance of about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth. The size of the Moon is much smaller than that of Earth. Its diameter is about 3,500 kilometres.
Interesting Information

Moon also rotates about its own axis. The duration in which it completes one trip around the Earth, it also completes one rotation about its own axis. That is why, we can see only the same one half of the surface of the Moon. We never see the other half.
Do you know?
The Moon completes one round around Earth in 27.3 days. Since the Earth is also moving, a complete round of Moon is completed for us in 29.5 days.
Ebb and Flow of Moon
Does the Moon have the same shape all the times? How does the Moon on Eid-ul-Fitar look like? On that day, what is the date of lunar month?
Ebb and Flow of Moon

The ebb and flow of the Moon in the sky is due to its rotation around the Earth. We see the side of moon which reflects sunlight to Earth. The other side of the moon is called dark side. On the first day of lunar month, we see very narrow sunlight on the edge of the Moon. This is called crescent. It is shown at position 1 in the figure.
Ebb and Flow of Moon

During its rotation around the Earth, it travels through position 2 to position 5. In this period, its size gradually increases. At position 5 it becomes full moon (badar). After this its bright part gradually decreases and eventually it disappears.
Do you know?
The Moon has no atmosphere. Moreover, there is no water on the Moon. That is why, no life exists on the Moon.
Interesting Information
All planets of Solar System have Moons except Mercury and Venus. Jupiter and Saturn have the maximum number of Moons.
Rotational Movement of Earth
Our Earth not only revolves in its orbit around the Sun but it also rotates about its own axis. The axis is an imaginary line that passes through the north and south poles of the Earth.
Rotational Movement of Earth
It is day at the part of the Earth, which is in front of the Sun. While it is night at the other part which is opposite to the Sun. The Earth completes one rotation around its axis in 24 hours.
Interesting Information
Day and night are due to the rotational motion of the Earth. The Earth rotates from west to east. This is the reason that the Sun appears to rise in the east and sets in the west.
Do you know?
Every planet is at a different distance from the Sun and revolves at different speed. Therefore, the duration of day is different on different planets.

Relation of Changing Shadows with Axial Rotation of Earth

During Earth's axial rotation, the Sun appears to rise in that part of the Earth that comes in front of the Sun. At this time, we see long shadows of trees and other objects. As the Earth keeps rotating, the shadows gradually decrease in size. At the noon, the shadow of any object is the smallest in size. On further rotation of the Earth, the size of shadows gradually increase in opposite direction.
Relation of Changing Shadows with Axial Rotation of Earth
Just before the Sun set, the shadows again become long as they were in the morning.

Relation of Changing Shadows with Axial Rotation of Earth
The size of shadows changes from long to short and then from short to long.
Annual Rotation of Earth around the Sun

The revolution of the Earth around the Sun is called orbital motion. The path of Earth's revolution around the Sun is almost circular. The Earth completes one revolution around the Sun in about 365 days. This period is called one year. The Earth's axis is tilted towards one side. Due to it, the Sun rays fall vertically at the northern hemisphere of the Earth.
Annual Rotation of Earth around the Sun
Therefore, the duration of day increases and that of night decreases there. Hence, it is summer season in the northern hemisphere.
Annual Rotation of Earth around the Sun
During the same time, the southern hemisphere of the Earth receives slanting Sun rays. Therefore, in this part, duration of day decreases and that of night increases and it is winter there.

Annual Rotation of Earth around the Sun
The annual rotation of the Earth and the tilt in its axis cause changes in seasons.
Lunar Eclipse

During the revolution of the Moon around the Earth, sometime the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon. Due to it, the sunlight does not reach the Moon. Therefore, a shadow of the Earth is formed on the Moon and it looks dark. This is called lunar eclipse.

Solar Eclipse

Sometime, during its revolution around the Earth, the Moon comes between the Earth and the Sun. In this condition, the Sun is hidden behind the Moon and is not visible from the Earth. A shadow of the Moon falls on the Earth. It is called solar eclipse.
Solar Eclipse

The complete solar eclipse is very rare. Usually, we see partial solar eclipses. It is because the Moon is much smaller than Earth. So, its shadow falls only at a small part of the Earth. Therefore, the solar eclipse can be seen only in those parts of the Earth.

Man lived in caves and forests thousands year ago. He started living in small settlements as he gained civility with the passage of time. Later on, these settlements developed into cities and states. To maintain its discipline, the administration came in the hands of government.
State

A specific area where humans live under a self-government with sovereignty is called a state. A state is basically formed of four elements: territory, population, government and sovereignty. It is the responsibility of a state to ensure the protection of the rights of its citizens and work for the development, prosperity and welfare of them.
Do you want to know more?

The foundation of the first Islamic state was laid by Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) in Madina Munawara. The basic principles of this Islamic state were the oneness of Allah, equality, sincerity and fear of Allah, receiving of knowledge and justice.
Do you want to know more?
Sovereignty is the supreme power of a state. The system of a state runs on the basis of this power. Almighty Allah holds the sovereignty as defined by the constitution of Pakistan.
Government

Government is the most important of the four elements of state. Government is such group of people which has the power to administer a country or a state. It is the responsibility of government to provide us the facilities of peace, health and means of transport. Ensure equities and justice and the provision of our rights as defined by the constitution.
Government
By fulfilling our needs, it should run the administration of a country.
Quotation

Pakistan is an Islamic democratic state which has specific geography and people live in this region. Government and state institutions are established to run its administration that perform its specific responsibilities and sovereignty rest with Almighty Allah.
For Teachers

Describe state and government to students with examples. Moreover, differentiate between the state, government and constitution. Tell the students about the importance of constitution. Furthermore, make the students aware of rights and responsibilities of citizens as defined by the constitution.
Difference between State and Government

There is a clear difference between state and government. State is formed of the four basic elements (Territory, Population, Government and Sovereignty). The concept of a state remains incomplete if any of the four elements is missing. On the other hand, government is one of the important elements of state. The administration of a state and the provision of equity and justice is not possible without government.
Difference between State and Government

The second difference between state and government is that the concept of state is permanent while governments are subject to change. For example, there is election of new representatives after some time in a democratic form of government. Hence another government is established in place of the previous government.
Difference between State and Government

The third major difference between a state and government is that the number of people in a state can be in millions but it is not necessary for all the people to be the part of government. There is an election of representatives from all the population to form a government.
Constitution

A set of basic principles for running the administrative discipline of a state or country is known as constitution. These principles are helpful in running the administration of government. All the laws of a country are made in the light of constitution.
Basic Characteristics of the 1973 Constitution
The present constitution of Pakistan was framed in 1973. Let us know about the basic characteristics of the constitution of Pakistan.
Basic Characteristics of the 1973 Constitution

All the supreme authority over the universe lies with Almighty Allah and every law be constituted in accordance with Quran and Sunnah. • According to the constitution, the name of Pakistan is "Islamic Republic of Pakistan". • The president and prime minister are obligatory to be Muslims and believe that there is no Rasool after Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم).
Basic Characteristics of the 1973 Constitution
• Islam is the state religion of the country. • The basic rights and responsibilities are also mentioned.
Do you want to know more?
The constituent assembly of the country framed the first constitution of Pakistan in 1956.

Rights

The right to live with freedom and protection • The right of equality and justice • The right of the basic facilities of life • The right of education • The right of freedom of expression • The right of vote
Responsibilities

To be loyal and patriotic with country • To take care of the rights of others • To abide by the laws and respect them • To pay taxes in time • To vote properly • To benefit the nation and country with skills and knowledge

For Teachers
For example, legislature constitutes laws, executive implements them and judiciary ensures that the implementation of these laws is performed for the public welfare.
Senate

The upper house in Pakistan is called Senate which represents all the provinces. Presently it has 104 members in Pakistan. Chairman of senate is elected from these members who presides the meeting of senate as well.
National Assembly

In Pakistan lower house is called National Assembly which performs on national level. Pakistan National Assembly presently has 342 members. Speaker presides the meeting of National Assembly. Members of National Assembly elect prime minister.
Do you want to know more?

Whenever there is need of a new law or to amend the existing law, there is detailed discussion on the bill in the national assembly. It is sent to the senate after the approval of national assembly for reconsideration. When the members of both the houses approve the bill, it is sent to the president. It becomes the law after the approval of president.
Do you want to know more?
Democratic system of government are of two types, parliamentary and presidential.
Executive

The implementation of laws made by legislature is performed by executive. Prime minister and its cabinet form executive. Prime minister is the head of federal government. Executive ensures the administration of various departments through ministries.

Liaquat Ali Khan was the first prime minister of Pakistan.

Judiciary performs to ensure the laws made by legislature and implemented by executive. It provides justice to the people by safeguarding their rights. Judiciary has the power to punish those who violate the law. Judiciary performs hearing of the cases through courts and explains the country laws.

Rule and Law

Some rules are designed to maintain peace in a society. For example we are often instructed by our elders to walk on road carefully whenever we go out of home and use the footpath. It is the rule for walking on road. Rules take the shape of law when issued by the government for all the citizens. Laws are same for all and abiding by it is the responsibility of every citizen.
Rule and Law
One who violates these laws deserves punishment.
Rules and Laws
Rules: Instructions that are useful for the people to live together and lead their lives safely. For example the rules for playground and classroom.
Rules and Laws
Laws: When rules are given the legal status, they are called laws. On the violation of laws, punishment is given, for instance, the laws of traffic and inheritance.
Democratic System of Government

Democracy is the most popular system of government all over the world. In fact, it is a government of the people, elected through votes of people and works for the people. Pakistan is an Islamic republic where democratic system of government exists. People here can raise a voice for their rights and freedom. A leader or head is required for running a democratic system of government.
Quotation
Democracy is the government of the people, by the people and for the people. (Abraham Lincoln)
Let's do something new!

Just as Pakistan has democratic system of government, similarly monarchy is also a system of government. A king or a queen has the administration of governing a country. For example, Saudi Arabia and Brunei have such system of government.
Qualities of a Leader
A few qualities of a leader are as under:
Qualities of a Leader

Planning for the betterment of country and people. • A leader understands the problems of people and tries to resolve them. • Popular among the public. • He shares the success with his entire team and appreciates their efforts. • A leader supervises the planning for its practical application.
Leader
A person who is leading as head of a group, organization, political party or a country is called a leader.
General Elections

The members of national and provincial assembly are elected in general elections. General election is an activity in which the public elects its representatives by using their right of vote. The elected representatives later on serve the country and nation realizing as their responsibilities.
General Elections
the Election Commission of Pakistan building
Do you want to know more?
Election Commission of Pakistan is an institution which has the responsibility to hold elections. Chief Election Commissioner is the head of this institution.
Political Parties

We often listen such talk shows on media where political parties are discussed. Individuals whose opinions and views about the country or state have similarities make a political party. These political parties gain popularity among the masses on the basis of their views and manifesto and sometimes participate in the elections.
Political Parties
The successful political party in the elections forms government and makes national policies. It resolves the public issues and works for the progress of country and nation.
I have learnt!

Government has three organs; legislature, executive and judiciary. • Some rules and laws are constituted for maintaining the law and order in a society. The one who violates the law deserves punishment. • Pakistan is an Islamic democratic state. Here Islamic democratic system of government exists. • General elections is a process where public elect their representatives by using their right of vote.
I have learnt!
• Every political party has its specific ideology and manifesto. Every political party has its leader.

Students Learning Outcomes
After completing this lesson students will be able to:
Students Learning Outcomes

Define History. • Identify early settlements and their areas. • Identify ancient civilizations along major rivers and coastal areas of the world (Mesopotamia, Nile Valley (Egyptian) and Indus Valley along with their timeline). • Describe the advent, lifestyle and decline of (Mesopotamia, Egyptian and Indus Valley).
Students Learning Outcomes

Early settlements of the world were established on the bank of rivers, where plenty of water was available which human beings used for their daily needs and irrigation. He could hunt fish from the rivers. He started making huts and homes from mud on the bank of river due to his dependence on water. These homes were used as permanent residence.
Students Learning Outcomes

Human beings found various metals later on and started making various tools first from bronze and then from iron. He got help in farming and hunting animals from these tools. Man progressed with the passage of time. He invented many objects and learnt new ways to live. His lifestyle got modernized and major civilizations began.
Students Learning Outcomes
The word civilization is derived from the words of Latin language "civitas" or "city".
Quotation
History is the study of past events which presents the record in a sequence.
Early Civilizations

There are many civilizations mentioned in the history of mankind which developed at different times and places. We will study the following civilizations in this lesson. Mesopotamia; Egyptian Civilization; Indus Valley Civilization.
Mesopotamia

Mesopotamia is one of the world's first civilizations. It began 3000 BC between rivers 'Tigris' and 'Euphrates', a fertile land, located in the south of Persian gulf and stretched upto Asia Minor and Armenia in the North. This area consisted of the modern time countries of Iraq, Turkey and Syria. This area consists of Sumerian, Assyria and Babylonian civilizations.
Mesopotamia

Therefore, Mesopotamia is called the cradle of civilizations. Large cities were developed here in which Babylon, Ashur and Nineveh were the most important. Every city of Mesopotamia had made its own god. In the middle of city a large Haikal of approximately 150 feet height minaret was constructed with straight four sides which were like a ladder. It was thought that gods came down here.
Mesopotamia

A regular system of government existed in Mesopotamia. They made many laws for leading lives. The people here adopted various professions like farming, livestock breeding and fishing etc. They were traders as well. The women here worked side by side with men.
Do you want to know more?

The name of 'fertile crescent' is given to a specific piece of land of Mesopotamia due to abundance of water and fertile soil. This area makes a shape like crescent on the map. The people of other areas came to live here due to its fertility.
For Teachers

Tell the students that history is the study of past events especially human matters. Tell them those people who study history and write about the past are called 'Historians'. Tell the students that the facilities of present time were not available in ancient time. Man really worked hard for survival. Tell them about the stone-age, bronze-age and iron-age.
Egyptian Civilization
The discoveries made in the peak days of Mesopotamia, changed the world. Among them mathematical concepts, wheel invention, yacht, maps and astronomical inventions are specially worth mentioning.
Egyptian Civilization

Mesopotamia was a large empire. It had many autocratic states but their emperors fought wars to occupy areas and lands of each other. The lives of common people were much affected due to these wars. The external people took advantage of these disturbances and Iranians and Greeks occupied Mesopotamia respectively.
Egyptian Civilization
The Greek warrior, Alexander the Great, conquered this land in 334 BC and brought an end to Mesopotamian government.
Quotation
The most ancient and early form of writing "Cuneiform" was in use in Mesopotamia. Reference: https://www.britannica.com/topic/cuneiform
Egyptian Civilization
a clay tablet covered with cuneiform writing
Egyptian Civilization

The Egyptian civilization developed on the bank of river Nile in Egypt. The relics of man lived thousands of years ago were found here. Settlements on a large scale began here, 3000 BC, approximately 5000 years ago. The search for water resources settled the man near the river Nile. Besides, river Nile was an important mean of transportation and commerce.
Egyptian Civilization

Fertile soil was brought in it by flood every year which made the plains of Nile valley fertile. The people living here cultivated food-grains. Wheat and barely were the important crops. Monarchy prevailed in ancient Egypt. The rulers were called 'Pharaoh'. These people preserved the corpses by putting special material on it which are called 'mummies'.
Egyptian Civilization
They made large graveyards and pyramids for keeping these mummies. These pyramids were decorated with the pictures of pharaohs and sculptures of gods.
Indus Valley Civilization
This civilization also declined as time passed. There were many reasons as:
Indus Valley Civilization

This civilization was occupied by other powers. • The unavailability of raw iron for making weapons. • Frequent civil wars. • The water level was very low in river Nile due to climatic changes. • Many people died due to drought, hunger and water shortage.
Quotation
Herodotus was an ancient Greek historian who called Egypt a gift of River Nile.
Pyramids of Egypt

Pyramids of Egypt especially the Giza pyramids are reckoned in the wonders of the world. In fact, these pyramids are the graveyard constructed by Pharaohs of Egypt. They believed in the life after death. They expected to become gods after death. Therefore, when a pharaoh died, he was buried in the pyramid along with golden and silver utensils, diamonds and jewels.
Pyramids of Egypt
Even now these pyramids exist in Egypt and are the part of the world's cultural heritage. People from across the world come to visit them.
Pyramids of Egypt
Sphinx — the great stone statue in front of a pyramid at Giza
Indus Valley Civilization

Indus valley civilization was developed about 2500 BC in the suburbs of River Indus. Pakistan, India and north eastern Afghanistan are the parts of this area. Indus Valley civilization included two big cities of Harappa, Mohenjo Daro and more than hundred small and large settlements.
Indus Valley Civilization

These people were called Dravidians. Most of the people were farmers, traders and skilled workers by profession. These people were also expert in carving and making clay pots. They had made big pots for the preservation of food grains. They made jewelry and tools from precious stones and metals. They had a regular system of measurement and weight.
Indus Valley Civilization

Dravidians worshipped animals, trees and statues. The stamps found in their cities were carved with the pictures of various animals. The pictures of elephants, rhinoceros, markhor, cows and bulls etc. are significant.
Indus Valley Civilization
a seal with a bull and script signs | a seal with an elephant; a seal with a humped bull | a seal with a rhinoceros
Indus Valley Civilization

The people of Indus valley were peace-loving. They had a little weapons of war. The Aryans entered the Indus valley about 1500 BC. They were nomads, grazing goats in Central Asia. They were warriors and had weapons of war. They occupied almost all the areas of Indus valley and killed many people. Some of the local people settled in the far flung areas of subcontinent to save their lives.
Indus Valley Civilization
It is guessed that their cities were drowned due to frequent flooding in river Indus so they settled in other areas leaving their own cities. Hence, Indus valley civilization declined.
Quotation
The ruins of Harappa were discovered in 1921 in Sahiwal, the city of Punjab. The ruins of Mohenjo Daro were discovered in 1922 near the city of Larkana in Sindh.
I have learnt!
History is the study of past events which presents the record in a sequence. • Mesopotamia, Egyptian and Indus Valley civilizations are the significant civilizations of past.

Students Learning Outcomes
Describe the key events (social and political) during the Life of Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) and Khalafat-e-Rashida.
Birth

Our Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) was born in 571 A.D in the famous city, Makkah, of Arab. His father's name was Hazrat Abdullah and his mother's name was Hazrat Aminah. His father Hazrat Abdullah, had died a few months before his birth.
Childhood

It was a custom among the respectable families of Arabs to send their newborn babies to villages so that they could be brought up in natural environment. Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) was also given to a pious lady, Bibi Halima. She nursed him for four years. She loved him very much and took care of him.
Childhood
When the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) was four years old, he was handed over to his mother, Hazrat Aminah.
Childhood
The Holy Nabi (ﷺ) now lived with his mother. But his mother also died after two years when he was only six years old.
Childhood

After the death of his mother, his grandfather, Hazrat Abdul Mutalib, started taking care of him. His grandfather was very aged. He also died after two years. After the death of his grandfather, he lived with his uncle, Hazrat Abu Talib. Hazrat Abu Talib loved him too much. He often gave him company in meal time and protected him.
Boyhood

When the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) grew up, his habits were very different from other youngsters. He (ﷺ) did not like playing in the streets the way other youngsters did. He (ﷺ) also kept himself away from bad people. At that time, Arab society had many evils. Instead of One Allah, they worshipped idols carved in stones. They buried their daughters alive. They often quarreled with each other.
Boyhood

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) hated these evils right from the beginning. He (ﷺ) always spoke truth and hated lies. This was the reason that people of Arab called him "Sadiq" and "Amin". When the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) was fifteen or sixteen years old, he (ﷺ) went to Palestine, Syria, Yemen and other remote areas for trade. He (ﷺ) was accompanied by his uncle.
Boyhood
His trade trip was very successful. He (ﷺ) earned great profit due to his honesty. The news of his honesty spread in the whole country.
Marriage

When a pious and rich Lady, Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا) heard about honesty of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ), she expressed her willingness to marry him. At that time, age of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) was 25 years while that of Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا) was 40 years. After seeking willingness of his uncle, the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) married Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا).
Nabowat

The Holy Nabi (ﷺ) often visited the cave of Hira in his youth. He (ﷺ) used to worship Allah there. When the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) was forty years old, one day he (ﷺ) was busy in his worship that Allah sent him an angel Hazrat Gabriel (علیہ السلام). The angel gave him happy news that Allah had chosen him as Nabi (ﷺ) to guide the people to the path of virtue and truth.
Nabowat

When the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) came to his home, he (ﷺ) told about the incident to his wife, Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا). She immediately believed in his Risalat. Later on, Hazrat Abu Bakar (رضی اللہ عنہ), Hazrat Ali (رضی اللہ عنہ) and Hazrat Zaid (رضی اللہ عنہ) also embraced Islam.
Preaching of Islam

The Holy Nabi (ﷺ) preached Islam silently for three years but during fourth year after the revelation of Risalat, the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) invited people of Makkah to accept Islam. The Holy Nabi (ﷺ) told them, Allah is One and they should worship only that One Allah. They should give up worshipping their idols. These idols could neither benefit nor harm them.
Preaching of Islam
They should avoid bad habits otherwise they would be cursed and punished by Allah.
Do you want to know more?

Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) worked out an agreement among the tribes of Madina which is the world's first written constitution. It is called 'Madina Charter'.
Hostility of the People of Makkah

People of Makkah did not want to hear anything against their idols. They became enemies of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) and his companions and troubled them in different ways. Sometimes they would throw stones at them or force them lay on hot sand or coal but despite all their hardships, the Muslims remained firm and no one gave up Islam.
Migration

When cruelties of the non-believers of Makkah exceeded the limits, the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) ordered the Muslims to migrate individually from Makkah to Madina. When the non-believers of Makkah came to know it, they decided to martyr the Holy Nabi (ﷺ). Allah ordered the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) through revelation to leave Makkah and migrate to Madina. Shifting of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madina is called migration (Hijrat).
The Conquest of Makkah

People of Madina treated the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) very well. He (ﷺ) continued preaching Islam. The non-believers of Makkah did not give up their mischiefs. They killed some men of the tribe which had supported the Muslims and waved swords in Haram-e-Kaaba.
The Conquest of Makkah

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) sent them a message to stop war, and pay ransom to the relatives of those who were killed. But the people of Makkah did not take the message seriously. The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) led his army of ten thousand men to Makkah.
The Conquest of Makkah

People of Makkah became worried when they heard about it. The People of Makkah surrendered without war except a brief fight at one place. Makkah was conquered without bloodshed. During the conquest of Makkah, the Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) forgave all the injustices done to him or his followers. He (ﷺ) ordered that no one should be victimized or plundered.
The Conquest of Makkah
Due to this order, people of Makkah embraced Islam truly.
The Last Pilgrimage (Hajj) of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ)

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) went to Makkah from Madina on 10th Hijri for performing Pilgrimage (Hajj). This was his last Pilgrimage (Hajj). Therefore, it is called the Last Pilgrimage (Hajj) or Hijat-ul-Wida. This time, a large number of Muslims had come with him to perform Hajj.
The Last Pilgrimage (Hajj) of the Holy Nabi (ﷺ)

On the occasion of Hajj, the Holy Nabi (ﷺ) gave them many advices and told them, "All Muslims are brothers to each other. There is no preference for Arab over non-Arab and the white over the black. Greater is the one who did good deeds and worshipped Allah".
Death

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) along with his companions returned to Madina after performing his last pilgrimage. A few days later he (ﷺ) became ill. The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) did not recover even though got treatment for illness.
Death
He (ﷺ) died on 12th Rabi-ul-Awwal, 11 Hijri, after his illness for fourteen days. His age was sixty three then.
The Pious Caliphs

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) is the last Nabi of Allah. After him, no other nabi will come till the Day of Judgment. Allah sent him as mercy for the whole world. This status was not given to any other nabi except Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم).
Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ)

Abdullah was the name of Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ). He was popularly known as "Abu Bakar". The title of Siddique was given to him by Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم). He was a close friend of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) since childhood. He was very truthful. Respectable families of Makkah treated him with great honour.
Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ)

He was the first among men to believe in his Risalat. Therefore, his status (position) was very high. After accepting Islam, he supported Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) in the time of trouble. He offered all his wealth for the glory of Islam. At the time of migration from Makkah to Madina, he spent three days with Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) in the cave of Sor. Thus he is also called the friend of Cave.
Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ)

It was he who paid price of the land bought for construction of Masjid-e-Nabwi. He was also blessed with the status of being given the responsibilities of leading Salah in the life time of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ).
Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ)

After the death of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ), all the Muslims elected him as Caliph unanimously. When he became Caliph, he told the Muslims: "O people, if I do good deeds, so follow me. But if I go the wrong way, then reform me. If I follow Allah and His Nabi (ﷺ), you should follow me. If I move away from the right path of Allah and His Nabi (ﷺ), then you are not bound to follow me."
Achievements

When Hazrat Abu Bakar (رضی اللہ عنہ) became caliph, the enemies of Islam had created many difficulties for the Muslims. There were some people who made false claims of Prophethood. Many people gave up giving Zakat. On this critical occasion, Hazrat AbuBakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ) acted very sensibly and courageously. He eradicated all those evils. Due to his efforts, Islam was saved from a great danger.
Achievements
Compilation of the Holy Quran is his great achievement. On the advice of Hazrat Umar (رضی اللہ عنہ) he compiled scattered parts of the Holy Quran and gave them the shape of Book.
Do you want to know more?

Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ) said in the first sermon of his Khalafat: "O people! I have been made your ruler but I am not better than you. The weak among you is strong for me until I give him his right and the strong among you is weak for me until I take the right due against him."
Character

Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ) was kind hearted, hospitable and brave. Inspite of being rich, he wore simple dress having many patches. He felt happiness in serving the needy and poor people. He went to the homes of blind and aged women to get them water.
Death

He worked hard day and night for the prosperity of Islam and Muslims. He lost his health and suffered from fever. At last, he died at the age of sixty three in 13 Hijri after remaining Caliph for two years and three months.
Hazrat Umar Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ)

Hazrat Umar Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ) was very brave. He was skilled in horsemanship, lance skill and archery. Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم) gave him the title of Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ).
Acceptance of Islam

In the beginning Hazrat Umar Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ) was against Islam. One day he stepped out of his home very angrily to martyr Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم). On the way he came to know from a man that his own sister and brother-in-law had also accepted Islam. When he heard it, he got more angered. He went to the house of his brother-in-law.
Acceptance of Islam

There he heard recitation of the Holy Quran. When he entered the house, he beat his sister and brother-in-law severely but they refused to give up Islam. He then told them that he also wanted to hear what they were reciting. When he heard some verses of the Holy Quran, his heart was deeply moved. He went straight to Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) and accepted Islam. His acceptance of Islam encouraged the Muslims.
Acceptance of Islam

The Muslims began offering prayers openly. After embracing Islam, he remained loyal to Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) till the last moment of his life. He took part in wars. He had such a deep love for Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) that when Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) passed away, he said that he would kill anyone talking about the death of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ).
Caliphate

After the death of Hazrat Abu Bakar Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ), Hazrat Umar Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ) was elected as Caliph. Islam made great progress during his period. Egypt, Syria, Iran and some other areas were conquered. Many reforms were implemented. He established courts for justice and appointed judges. A department was established for keeping peace and protecting lives and property of people.
Caliphate
Canals, wells and lakes were built for the development of agriculture. Department of Postal Service was established. Census was started.
Character

He was pious and lover of justice. He always feared Allah. He always worried about happiness of his subjects. He visited streets of the city during night in disguise. If he found a person in trouble, he helped him/her. After Juma Prayer, he sat in the courtyard of the Masjid to hear complaints of his people and would solve their problems. He served Islam immensely.
Character
Someone has rightly said that if another Umar (رضی اللہ عنہ) had been born, people of the whole world would have been Muslims.
Do you want to know more?

Inspite of being the caliph of a very large empire, Hazrat Umar Farooq (رضی اللہ عنہ) wore very simple dress which had patches in it, ate simple food which a common Muslim ate and even during journey, used blanket etc. as shade under a tree instead of a tent.
Death
On the tenth year of caliphate, a slave attacked him with a dagger and wounded him. The wound was deep due to which he passed away at the age of sixty three.
Hazrat Usman (رضی اللہ عنہ)

Hazrat Usman (رضی اللہ عنہ) also belonged to the tribe of Quraish. He is also one of the earliest believers in the Risalat of Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین صلی اللہ علیہ وعلیٰ آلہ واصحابہ وسلم). He was a trader. He always spent his wealth generously for serving Islam. Therefore, he is called 'Ghani' (the generous). Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) loved him too much.
Hazrat Usman (رضی اللہ عنہ)

He married two daughters of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) Hazrat Ruqayya (رضی اللہ عنہا) and Hazrat Umme Kalsoom (رضی اللہ عنہا), one after the other. Thus Hazrat Usman (رضی اللہ عنہ) is also called 'Zunnurain'.
Caliphate

He was appointed caliph after Hazrat Umar (رضی اللہ عنہ). He was the third caliph of the Muslims. During his caliphate, Muslims conquered many countries and Islamic state expanded vastly. He did a lot for the betterment of Muslims and his subjects. He constructed roads and inns. He dug wells for drinking water. His great achievement is construction and extension of Masjid-e-Nabwi. He also added naval forces to army.
Do you want to know more?
A few characteristics of Khalafat of Hazrat Usman (رضی اللہ عنہ):
Do you want to know more?

Provision of job opportunities to all the people without any personal or class discrimination. • The right for everyone to complain directly to the ruler. • Permanent and continuous accountability of the authorities and officials.
Character

He was famous for his modesty, wisdom, politeness and kindness. His position is also greater in terms of generosity. He bought many salves and set them free. He bought a well of drinking water for eight thousand dinar from a Jew for Muslims. Most of his time was spent in recitation of the Holy Quran.
Martyrdom

He was very kind hearted. Some evil minded people tried to misuse his kindness for illegal advantages. He forbade them and they turned against him. They made mischievous deeds. Hazrat Ali (رضی اللہ عنہ) and other Muslims made those evil-minded people understand but the advice had no effect on them. One day he was reciting the Holy Quran in his home, they attacked and martyred him.
Hazrat Ali (رضی اللہ عنہ)

Role of Provinces/Regions in the Creation of Pakistan

Pakistan is a federation including Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, Kashmir, Gilgit Baltistan and Islamabad. Every region of Pakistan fully contributed in the movement of Pakistan. Let us know about their role in the creation of Pakistan.
Role of Sindh

Muhammad Bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712 A.D and the preaching of Islam began in subcontinent. The message of Islam spread from this region to the rest of the parts of Indo-Pak subcontinent. That is the reason Sindh is also called the gateway of Islam. The history of Sindh shows that after the occupation of British, the people here never accepted the British rule.
Role of Sindh

Sindh played an important role in the Pakistan Movement. Sindh was the first province which passed the resolution of a Muslim state. This resolution was presented by Sheikh Abdul Majeed Sindhi in Sindh Assembly.
Role of Sindh

Sibghatullah Shah Rashdi was an active leader of Pakistan Movement in Sindh. He raised the voice against the British occupation of subcontinent. Quaid-e-Azam also belonged to Sindh. He raised the voice for the protection of rights of Muslims in Sindh and activated the Sindh Muslim League.
Role of Sindh

Besides him, Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah, Sir Abdullah Haroon, Ghulam Hussain Hidayatuallah, Mir Bande Ali Talpur and Muhammad Ayub Khoro were also active leaders of Sindh. The students of Sindh also actively participated in Pakistan Movement. The students of Noor Muhammad High School Hyderabad and Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam Karachi also played their role in the movement for Pakistan.
Role of Sindh

Sindh assembly passed a resolution in favour of Pakistan Resolution on 3rd March 1943. Sindh assembly decided to join the constituent assembly of Pakistan on 26th June 1947. In this way, Sindh became the first province which joined Pakistan.

Allama Muhammad Iqbal belonged to Punjab. He presented the concept of Pakistan and made the Muslims demand for freedom through his poetry. Besides him, Sir Muhammad Shafi, Malik Barkat Ali and Begum Jehan Ara Shahnawaz were the prominent leaders of Punjab.
Role of Punjab

The Muslim leaders of Punjab decided to unite on a single platform so that the Muslims can get their separate identity. They strengthened Punjab Muslim League for this purpose. Pakistan Resolution was also presented in Lahore for the demand of a separate homeland on March 23, 1940. The Minar-e-Pakistan was constructed in Lahore in memory of this resolution.
Role of Punjab
Minar-e-Pakistan is the symbol of our struggle for independence.

The old name of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is North West Frontier Province. This region has been very important due to its strategic location since ancient times. Khyber Pass, located in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, remained an important trade passage and military point of the world for a long time. Alexander the Great, the Greek ruler also entered Indo-Pak subcontinent through this passage.
Role of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

The people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa are very courageous and freedom-lovers. That is the reason that they never accepted the British dominance. The people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa actively participated in the movement for Pakistan. Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar was an important character of Pakistan Movement.
Role of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

He remained the member of the constituent assembly of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa from 1937 to 1945 and he also performed the duties of Finance Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (1943 to 1945). Role of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

A referendum for the future of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was held in July 1947 when the freedom of subcontinent was announced on June 3, 1947. Majority of the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa decided to join Pakistan in this referendum.
Role of Balochistan

The people of Balochistan are freedom lovers. They were always against the British dominance. Balochistan was a very backward area of Indo-Pak subcontinent. The movement for Pakistan started very late as compared to other provinces. A legal advisor, Qazi Muhammad Isa, on the instruction of Quaid-e-Azam strengthened Muslim League in Balochistan in 1939.
Role of Balochistan
